1. A watch means tornadoes are possible: stay close to a sturdy building and keep NOAA Weather Radio or local broadcasts on. A warning means one is occurring or minutes away: take shelter at once.
2. Know the signs, because some tornadoes form too fast to warn: a rotating funnel, an approaching cloud of debris, large hail, a dark and often greenish sky, or a roar like a freight train.
3. Best shelter: an underground shelter, a basement or storm cellar, or a safe room built to FEMA P-361 or ICC 500. Next best: a small, windowless interior room or hallway on the lowest floor, with as many walls as possible between you and outside. Get under something sturdy, cover your head and neck, and wear a helmet if one is to hand. Leave the windows shut; opening them does nothing.
4. Mobile homes are not safe, even tied down. Leave for the nearest sturdy building now, and decide before the season which building that is.

Emergency Alert System
The screeching tones on radio and TV are the EAS, relayed by every broadcaster and cable system. The same data bursts drive weather radio alarms. It carries weather warnings, civil emergencies and Amber alerts, and it only reaches you while you are tuned in and the station is on the air.
Wireless Emergency Alerts on phones
WEA messages come by cell broadcast to every phone on a tower, free, with their own alarm tone even when the ringer is off. They cover tornado, flash flood, hurricane, extreme wind, tsunami and destructive thunderstorm warnings, Amber alerts and local emergencies. You can switch off most categories in the phone's settings; National Alerts cannot be disabled. Leave them on. They need a working tower and a charged phone, which is exactly what you may not have.
Elsewhere
Outside the United States, find your national weather service's warning channel (broadcast radio, an app, SMS or cell broadcast) and a battery radio that carries it. The watch and warning logic is the same.

passages.text:
Before the season
1. Learn whether you live in an evacuation zone. Zones are drawn for storm surge, the rise in sea level that has caused about nine in ten tropical cyclone deaths. Plan to leave if officials say so, if you live in a mobile home or on a floodplain, if your house has no storm strengthening, or if past storms brought surge damage.
2. Plan both options: a destination and route tens of kilometres inland if you leave, and a small, interior, windowless room on the lowest level that will not flood if you stay.
3. Gather at least three days of supplies, including medicines and what pets need. Keep documents somewhere safe or as password-protected copies. Buy flood insurance; standard policies do not include it.
4. Prepare the house for wind and water: clear drains and gutters, fit check valves to stop backups, consider shutters, trim or remove damaged limbs, and check the roof, windows and doors.
When a storm is coming
1. Track the forecast and expect it to change. Fill the car, charge phones, and if you are leaving, leave early. If you are not in a zone and not in a mobile home, staying put keeps you out of the gridlock that shadow evacuations cause.
2. If told to evacuate, go immediately and never drive around barricades.
3. Public shelters are the last resort. They are first come, first served, built to protect life from wind and water and not always stocked with food, water or bedding, and they usually take only service animals.
During and after
1. Stay in your safe room through the storm. If flooding traps you, go up, but not into a closed attic.
2. Afterwards, treat floodwater, downed lines and debris as in Flood, and the house as in Returning home.

1. Go back only when local authorities say it is safe. On the way, watch for washed-out roads, downed lines and debris, and report chemical spills, smouldering insulation, downed wires and dead animals to the authorities.
2. Outside first. Walk around the building with a torch, never a flame, looking for loose or downed power lines, the smell of gas, floodwater around the building, and structural damage: cracks in walls, doors and windows out of square, a shifted foundation, chimney damage. If you find any of these, or the house had fire damage that no official has inspected, do not go in; ask for a building inspector or structural engineer.
3. Gas. If you smell gas or hear hissing or blowing, open a window and leave immediately. Only professionals turn the supply back on. No smoking, candles, oil or gas lanterns or flame torches until you are sure there is no leaking gas.
4. Electricity. Do not touch the electrical system if you are wet, standing in water or unsure. Turn off the main breaker if you can do it safely, unplug wet appliances and let them dry, and have an electrician check the wiring and the appliances before the power goes back on.
5. Water and food. Expect a boil-water notice and check with the water authority. Fridge food is safe after an outage of up to four hours if the door stayed shut; throw away perishables that have been above 4 °C (40 °F) for more than two hours, anything that touched floodwater or fire, and refrigerated medicines after more than a day without power unless the label says otherwise.
6. Pump out a flooded basement slowly, about a third of the water a day; walls can collapse and floors buckle if you empty it while the ground outside is still saturated. Open cupboards carefully, and expect mice, rats, snakes and insects that came in with the water.

Signs of a release: coloured smoke or mist, oily dark patches on leaves or ground, a strange taste in food or water, sick or dying animals and birds, and in people watering eyes, coughing, choking, dizziness, itching or burning skin. Many agents have no colour or smell, and if you can smell chlorine or ammonia you are already breathing a harmful dose.
2. Outdoors, leave crosswind first, then upwind, on high ground. Most toxic gases are heavier than air and pool in cellars, ditches, gullies and valleys, and woods and tall grass hold the vapour.
3. If officials say shelter in place: go inside, shut windows, vents and dampers, turn off fans and air conditioning, and seal an interior room above ground (see Sheltering in place). A chemical plume disperses within hours.
4. If anything got on you, take off the contaminated clothing away from other people, bag it, and rinse skin and hair with plenty of water and soap. Vapour trapped in cloth keeps gassing off onto whoever stands nearby. For a vapour exposure the first treatment is fresh air.
5. A wet T-shirt or cloth over the nose and mouth is an escape filter only; it is not protection to stay in.
6. Breathing trouble can be delayed. Chlorine, ammonia and phosgene (made when solvents, foam plastics and non-stick coatings burn) can swell the airway or fill the lungs hours after the exposure. Anyone with chest tightness or shortness of breath afterwards should rest, avoid exertion and get medical care.
7. Do not use wood or plants from a contaminated area for fire, food or water. Check water sources for oil films, odd smells and dead fish, and keep food and water covered.
8. On a tanker or rail car the diamond placard gives the hazard class (flammable, toxic gas, corrosive and so on) and a UN number that responders look up. Read it from a distance; do not approach to read it.

Someone collapses and is not breathing normally
1. Check for a response and breathing (no more than 10 seconds). Shout for help and have someone call emergency services and fetch a defibrillator (AED) if one exists.
2. Kneel beside them, heel of one hand on the centre of the chest, other hand on top. Push hard and fast: 5 to 6 cm deep, 100 to 120 per minute, letting the chest come fully back up.
3. If trained, give 30 compressions then 2 breaths (tilt head, lift chin, pinch nose, one-second breaths that make the chest rise). If not trained or unwilling, do compressions only without stopping.
4. When an AED arrives, turn it on and follow its voice prompts; keep compressing while the pads go on.
5. Swap rescuers every two minutes. Stop only when they breathe normally, help takes over, or you cannot continue.
Choking
1. If they can cough or speak, encourage coughing and stay with them.
2. If they cannot breathe, cough or speak: give 5 back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand, then 5 abdominal thrusts (stand behind, fist just above the navel, pull sharply in and up). Alternate until the object comes out.
3. For a pregnant or very large person use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts. For an infant under one year, use 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts with two fingers; never abdominal thrusts.
4. If they become unresponsive, start CPR. Look in the mouth before each set of breaths and remove anything you can see.

1. Natural gas has no smell of its own; suppliers add an odorant so a leak smells of rotten eggs. Learn now where the gas meter and the main shut-off valve are, and keep the wrench it needs beside it.
2. If you smell gas or hear hissing or blowing from a pipe or appliance: do not switch anything on or off, do not light anything, and do not use a phone indoors. Open a window if it is on your way, get everyone out, and leave the door open behind you.
3. Call the gas utility or emergency services from outside, well away from the building, and do not go back in until they say so.
4. Turn the gas off at the meter only if you can do it safely and you know how. Once it is off, leave it off. Only the utility or a professional should turn the supply back on and relight appliances.
5. After an earthquake, flood or fire, check for the smell of gas before you go inside. No smoking and no candles, oil or gas lanterns or flame torches for light until you are sure there is no leaking gas or other flammable material.
6. Bottled propane and butane are odorised the same way. Treat the smell the same way, and keep cylinders outdoors.
A gas detector does not replace your nose, and carbon monoxide is a different hazard with a different alarm (see Carbon monoxide).

1. A sound coop is the preparation: predator-proof wire mesh, dry, ventilated, with perches and nest boxes, on well-drained ground sheltered from the prevailing wind. Shut the birds in at night; predators take free-ranging birds.
2. Water first. Excess heat, cold or damp all harm the birds, so check and refill drinkers often, break ice in a freeze and give shade and extra water in heat.
3. Store feed dry in sealed bins that rodents cannot open. Free-ranging hens find much of their own food, and village hens have lived for months on scavenging and still laid an egg or two a week, so a short gap in bought feed is survivable; expect laying to fall.
4. Keep wild birds away from the flock's feed and water. Avian influenza passes from wild birds, and a closed run cuts the risk. If several birds die suddenly, report it and do not handle them bare-handed.
5. Salmonella: wash hands after handling birds, eggs or the coop, keep coop boots and tools out of the house, keep children's hands washed, collect eggs daily and cook them well.
6. Lead and other metals in soil end up in eggs. Do not site a run beside old painted buildings or on suspect ground.
7. If you evacuate, a ventilated box carries a few hens; otherwise leave them shut in the coop with as much feed and water as you can set out.
8. After a wildfire or flood keep the birds penned off burned or flooded ground; ash holds heat pockets and floodwater carries contamination.

passages.text:
Where
1. Never inside the house, the basement or any room with a furnace, water heater or pilot light. A detached shed or a ventilated outbuilding, out of the sun, away from the dwelling and from anything that sparks.
2. Follow your local fire code and insurer on quantity; many limit what may be kept at a home. Keep an extinguisher nearby and nothing flammable stacked around the fuel.
Petrol (gasoline)
Stored well, petrol stays good for about six months, and a year-old can will usually still run an engine. Stale fuel gums carburettors and injectors.
Use approved fuel containers only, kept more than half full and tightly capped so the light fractions cannot evaporate and moisture cannot get in. Fuel with ethanol absorbs water from the air and can separate into layers; keep it sealed and use it sooner.
Add a fuel stabiliser when you fill the can, and run any stored engine for ten minutes afterwards so treated fuel reaches the carburettor. Run stored engines at intervals to purge stale fuel.
Rotate: label each can with the date, pour the oldest into the car on a schedule, and refill. Fill cans on the ground, never in a vehicle or on a truck bed. Petrol vapour ignites at any temperature you will meet and spreads along the ground.
Propane (LPG)
Propane is stored as a liquid under pressure; the hazards are leaks and heat, not staleness. Store cylinders outdoors, upright, valve closed, out of direct sun and never in a basement, garage or vehicle. Propane is heavier than air: a leak drifts across the floor to the nearest pilot light.
It smells of rotten eggs by design. If you smell it, no switches, no flames; get out and close the valve from outside if you can. Cylinders are filled only to about 80 percent so the liquid can expand in heat; never overfill one.
Check hoses and fittings for leaks with soapy water each season. Retire rusty or dented cylinders.
Kerosene
Store only clear 1-K kerosene for heaters and lamps, in a container never used for petrol. Even a trace of petrol in kerosene can make a heater or lamp explode.

question: well got flooded, how much bleach to shock it and how long before we can drink from it

passages.text:
Look first at what you already have
1. The water heater tank, toilet cisterns (not the bowl), ice cubes and the pipes (open the highest tap, then drain the lowest) hold tens of litres.
2. Rain is the cleanest free source. Put out every clean container, and run a tarp or gutter downspout into a covered barrel. Discard the first flush off a dirty roof.
In the open
1. Move downhill and towards greener vegetation; streams, springs and seeps collect in valleys. Flowing water beats standing water.
2. Collect dew before sunrise by dragging an absorbent cloth through grass and wringing it into a container.
3. Melt snow or ice in small amounts added to a little water already in the pot; eating snow cools you and costs energy.
4. Build a solar still where there is sun but no surface water: a plastic sheet over a pit with a container under the sag point.
Never drink seawater, urine, blood or water from near latrines, dumps or downstream of livestock. Treat everything you collect (see Boil, bleach, filter), including rainwater that has run over a roof.
passages.title: Finding water when the taps are dry

passages.text:
1. Do not drink from a flooded well until it has been disinfected and tested. Use stored, bottled or boiled water meanwhile.
2. Turn off power to the pump. Remove the well cap or vent plug and clear debris from around the casing. If the pump or wiring was under water, have an electrician check it first.
3. Mix plain unscented bleach with water in a clean bucket. The amount depends on the casing diameter and water depth: a common rule is about 1 litre (1 quart) of 5 to 9 percent bleach per 100 US gallons of water in the well, and your state or county health department publishes exact tables.
4. Pour the mix into the well, then run a garden hose from an outside tap back into the casing until the water smells strongly of chlorine, washing down the inside of the casing.
5. Open every tap in the house until chlorine is smelled at each, then close them. Replace the cap and let the system stand 12 to 24 hours. Do not drink, bathe in or give animals this water.
6. Flush through an outside hose away from the septic system, lawn and streams until the chlorine smell is gone, then flush the indoor taps.
7. Have the water tested for bacteria one to two weeks later and again a month on. Keep treating or using an alternative supply until two clean tests.
Chlorine does not fix chemical contamination (fuel, pesticides, nitrate). A well that was submerged by flood water carrying fuel needs professional assessment.
passages.title: Shock-chlorinating a private well after a flood

passages.text:
If you can boil
1. Let cloudy water settle, then pour it through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter.
2. Bring it to a rolling boil for one minute. Above 2,000 m (6,500 ft), boil for three minutes.
3. Let it cool covered and store it in clean, covered containers. A pinch of salt per litre improves the flat taste.
If you cannot boil, use bleach
1. Use plain, unscented household bleach (5 to 9 percent sodium hypochlorite). No splashless, scented or colour-safe products.
2. Add 2 drops per litre (8 drops, a little under 1/8 teaspoon, per US gallon) of clear water. Double the dose for cloudy water.
3. Stir and wait 30 minutes. A faint chlorine smell means the dose was enough. If there is no smell, repeat the dose and wait 15 more minutes.
Filters
Most portable filters remove parasites and bacteria. Only filters labelled for viruses remove them, so pair a filter with boiling or bleach when sewage may be in the water.
Boiling, bleach and filters do not remove fuel, pesticides, heavy metals or other chemicals. If water smells of chemicals or an authority says it is chemically contaminated, use bottled or stored water instead.
passages.title: Boil, bleach, filter: making water safe to drink
